articles.title: Asking Your Bank About Sending Money to Cuba Isn’t the Same as Ordering a Transfer: What OFAC Clarifies - CubaHeadlines
articles.summary: Asking Your Bank About Sending Money to Cuba Isn’t the Same as Ordering a Transfer: What OFAC Clarifies  CubaHeadlines
articles.full_text:
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) within the U.S. Department of the Treasury provides a straightforward clarification for those worried that inquiring with their about sending money to Cuba might have repercussions: posing a question does not equate to initiating a payment, and this distinction is crucial.
This is outlined in OFAC's FAQ 53, last updated on October 26, 2026, although it was initially released in January 2015. It remains unclear what specific text was updated or if the underlying regulation has changed.
According to this document, when a customer approaches their bank with the question, "Can I send money to Cuba?", the financial institution can either provide a direct response or refer the individual to OFAC's compliance line for further guidance. In this scenario, there is no transaction to block or reject, and the bank is under no obligation to file a report with the regulatory body.
The situation changes dramatically if the customer gives specific payment instructions. Should these instructions involve a blocked person, the bank must freeze the funds and notify OFAC via the agency's Reporting System within ten business days of the property becoming blocked.
When a transfer is prohibited but does not involve a blockable interest—meaning the recipient is not on the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List or other blocked categories—the bank must reject the transaction and submit the appropriate rejection report, as outlined in OFAC's FAQ 36, also updated this week.
A commonly misunderstood point is that not all Cubans are individually blocked. OFAC notes that certain categories may be blocked without appearing by name on the SDN, yet the legality of each remittance depends on the specific beneficiary, involved intermediaries, the type of transaction, and applicable licenses. This distinction does not imply that all remittances to Cuba are either authorized or prohibited.
Familial remittances from the United States to Cuba remain legally permissible under regulation 31 C.F.R. § 515.570, provided the recipient is not a prohibited Cuban government official or a banned Communist Party member, and the transaction does not involve entities on the Cuba Restricted List (CRL).
The operational landscape, however, has become increasingly complex. Western Union indefinitely halted its transfers from the United States to Cuba in February 2025, following the addition of its Cuban operator, Orbit S.A., to the CRL.
As of September 30, 2026, new sanctions stemming from Executive Order 14404 have expanded restrictions on indirect transactions with entities on this list and eliminated "U-turn" operations related to Cuba.
Additionally, since January 1, 2026, a federal tax of 1% applies to international remittances paid in cash, money orders, or cashier's checks, although it does not apply to bank transfers or payments made with U.S. credit or debit cards.
Individuals seeking specific guidance before attempting any transaction are encouraged to contact OFAC's compliance line at 1-800-540-6322, a resource to which the agency directs inquiries when a bank cannot directly resolve them.
OFAC emphasizes that making this call, or posing the question at a bank branch, does not trigger any blocking mechanisms or create a reporting obligation.
Understanding OFAC Regulations on Cuban Remittances
What is OFAC's stance on asking banks about sending money to Cuba?
Are all transactions to Cuba prohibited by OFAC?
Not all transactions to Cuba are prohibited. The legality of each transaction depends on the specific beneficiary, intermediaries involved, type of transaction, and applicable licenses.
What happens if a bank receives specific payment instructions for a blocked person?
If a bank receives specific payment instructions involving a blocked person, it must freeze the funds and report to OFAC within ten business days.

articles.title: DHS Updates UFLPA Entity List with Three Companies Engaged in Genetics Testing - Thompson Hine
articles.summary: DHS Updates UFLPA Entity List with Three Companies Engaged in Genetics Testing  Thompson Hine
articles.full_text:
On October 28, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the addition of three Chinese companies to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List. Effective October 29, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will apply a rebuttable presumption that goods produced in whole or part by these three companies are made with forced labor and prohibited from entering the United States.
According to a press release by DHS, the three Chinese genomics companies help the government of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region build and operate its mass surveillance infrastructure. The three entities added to the UFLPA Entity List are related companies – Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd. (BGI Group) is the controlling shareholder of BGI Genomics Co., Ltd. MGI Tech Co., Ltd. is under the control of the same ultimate controlling shareholder as BGI Group.
DHS has issued an updated UFLPA Entity List. For general background information on the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA), see Thompson Hine’s International Trade Update of June 2022. In addition, CBP’s UFLPA Dashboard containing current statistics and is available here.

articles.title: Hive ransomware affiliate jailed, years after FBI infiltrated the gang’s systems
articles.summary:
A Ukrainian man who carried out ransomware attacks for both the Nefilim and Hive gangs, including attacks on law firms and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic, has been sentenced to 70 months in a US prison.

Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.
articles.full_text:
A Ukrainian man has been sentenced to 70 months in a US prison for his role in a series of ransomware attacks.
36-year-old Artem Stryzhak became an affiliate of the Nefilim ransomware group around June 2021, receiving an 80% cut of the ransoms he managed to extort in attacks against hospitals, government organisations, law firms, and businesses around the world.
The rest of the ransom would go to Nefilim's administrators - including fellow Ukrainian Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who was charged last year in relation to attacks against hundreds of corporate victims using the LockerGoga and MegaCortex ransomware, as well as Nefilim.
At the time of writing, Tymoshchuk is not in US custody and a US $11 million bounty has been offered by the US State Department for information leading to his arrest.
Nefilim was not the only ransomware gang that Stryzhak worked closely with. He was also an early affiliate of the Hive ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation which targeted businesses and, in particular, organisations working in healthcare.
The FBI later warned that Hive had extorted US $100 million from businesses and organisations globally in a period of just 18 months.
According to the US Department of Justice, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators were behind Hive ransomware attacks against a number of victims, including law firms, a dentist's office, and a healthcare provider, during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector.
In January 2023, it was revealed that a multinational law enforcement operation had secretly penetrated the Hive ransomware operation in late July 2022, capturing decryption keys and quietly passing them to victims so they did not have to pay a ransom.
The DOJ said that the operation saved corporate victims of Hive over US $130 million in ransom payments.
At the time I speculated that the take-down of Hive may lead to the identification and possible apprehension of some of those involved in Hive ransomware attacks. In June 2024, Stryzhak was arrested in Barcelona, and subsequently extradited to the United States where he pleaded guilty.
The infiltration into Hive's infrastructure took place in 2022. Stryzhak was arrested in 2024, and sentenced in 2026. If there's a lesson for ransomware affiliates who think they got away with it, it's that law enforcement is prepared to be patient, and the evidence does not go away.
That's something that Volodymyr Tymoshchuk may also want to consider.

articles.full_text:
Dutch spies, Russian hackers and Jared Kushner’s iPhone. It sounds like the ingredients for a thriller, but according to claims in a new book the US President's son-in-law may have been hacked twice. Is any of it true, and what does it tell us about the phones in our pockets?

Meanwhile, James Ball explains that of the internet’s most trusted security keys were protected by numbers so small that one of them was... four. Yes, "4". And then, of course, to make the week worse we suffered a PHPocalpyse...

Plus, Chuck Randolph of 360 Privacy explains how the internet has made it scarily easy to put company executives and public officials in danger.

All this and more in episode 490 of the “Smashing Security” podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest James Ball.

articles.title: Hackers leak personnel data of 41,000+ Homeland Security staff, including ICE and border agents
articles.summary:
The US Department of Homeland Security has had the details of more than 41,000 staff, including ICE and CBP agents, published online. Not ideal for an organisation with "Security" in its name.

Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.
articles.full_text:
More than 41,000 people working for the US Department of Homeland Security, including ICE agents, have had their details published online by a group of hacktivists.
As TechCrunch reports, the leaked records include the names, job titles, work email addresses, phone numbers, abd office locations.
More than half of the leaked records relate to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, typically found at airports, seaports, and land border crossings. Around 10,000 ICE employees have had their records breached, and almost 1,000 members of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).
WIRED reports that the massive leak includes staff who work undercover, as well as in other sensitive areas such as those engaged in wiretapping and the interception of communications.
A hacktivist group calling itself "Department of Peace" says that the data was taken from an Okta single sign-on system that staff use to log onto the central network of the US Department of Homeland Security. Okta for its part says that it has not seen any evidence that its own systems have been compromised.
The data reveals which tools and services particularly individuals can access. Alongside everyday office software, these include Palantir's Falcon investigative platform, the phone and social media analysis tool PenLink, and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition app used by immigration agents.
Explaining its justification for the data breach, "Department of Peace" wrote:
"They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs."
The leaked data has been published online, under the title "Icepick", and can be either downloaded via a torrent or accessed via a web interface - making it significantly easier for curious parties to search.
One threat intelligence expert told WIRED that, if authentic, the leaked data was "an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS," and could help adversaries identify vulnerable personnel or compromise ongoing investigations.
An obvious concern is that the leaked contact details could be used in phishing attacks that target employees, or could potentially put agents in physical danger. Clearly anyone whose details have been exposed through the incident would be wise to treat unexpected emails, texts, and phone calls with caution - and be particularly wary of any communications that claim to come from IT support or ask for a login to be approved.
Earlier this year the same group of hacktivists claimed to have breached the US Department of Homeland Security and accessed contracts between DHS, ICE, and more than 6000 firms including the likes of L3Harris, Raytheon, Palantir, Microsoft, and Oracle.
Explaining their motivation for that breach, the hackers referred to the killings of Alex Pretti and Renée Good by federal agents in Minneapolis.
"Why hack the DHS? I can think of a couple Pretti Good reasons! I'm releasing this because the DHS is killing us and people deserve to know which companies support them and what they're working on."
There has been a long string of cybersecurity incidents affecting US government personnel. For instance, in September the notorious ShinyHunters hacking group claimed to have stolen personal details related to nearly every employee of the FBI, and the records of millions of serving and former US military personnel were reportedly stolen from the Pentagon's human resources unit.

articles.summary:

articles.full_text:
This story is interesting:
One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about.
Among the pre-installed bloatware—­or spyware, if you’re being less charitable­—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go.
It’s interesting because it exposes all the insecurities in this piece of IoT software. But I think the real story is that a random person was able to do this reverse-engineering with the help of AI. Expect a lot more stories like this in the future.
